utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before we go into the proper business of this Court, you will observe that we are sitting in the absence of Judge Moloto. He is sadly absent by reason of urgent personal business in South Africa, his mother having passed away during the Easter holiday. In the circumstances, Judge Hoepfel and I, the other members of the Chamber, have made an order pursuant to Rule 15 bis in the interest of justice to proceed in his absence in consideration of not only a fair, but an expeditious trial. And in those circumstances, we sit sadly in the absence of Judge Moloto. Before we proceed into the substantive business of the Court, there is an outstanding housekeeping matter, and it concerns two Defence exhibits, namely Exhibit 111 and Exhibit 112. On the 3rd of February, 2006, the Prosecution, having taken an objection, the parties agreed that the title of Exhibit 111, "Croats on their way, UN on the run" is not part of the evidence. The parties further agreed that the title of Exhibit 112, "The morale of the troops,' is not part of the evidence. The Trial Chamber would therefore like to correct the orders by way of a redaction of Exhibits 111 and 112 accordingly and the Chamber is requesting that the correct versions be put in place before Friday, the 28th of April, 2006. So could we please have that done in a timely manner, Mr. Whiting and Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. As they are Defence exhibits, I don't know if Mr. Milovancevic wants us undertake the redactions or if he would like us to deal with them. We're happy to deal with them either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will do that, Your Honour. Thank you. It is our exhibit, and we have fully agreed with the submission that the original headlines were not part of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine with the Prosecution. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First, on behalf of the Prosecution I would like to express our condolences to Judge Moloto. He is obviously not present to receive them. We will express them more directly when he returns, but our thoughts are, of course, with him during this sad time and we are sorry he is not present with us. Before we call our next witness, who is Ambassador Peter Galbraith, there is just a procedural matter to raise with respect to his testimony. As the Court is aware, an order was entered on the 13th of January 2006 with respect to this witness, with respect to particular measures. As the Court is aware, this witness is testifying about matters that he observed and heard and was aware of in his capacity as the United States Ambassador to Croatia. His testimony is being received under a waiver of Rule 70 by the United States government, and certain conditions have been imposed. The first -- and these have been ordered by the Court. The first, of course, is that the cross-examination must be restricted to the scope of the direct examination, and the topics that are covered on the direct examination have been carefully prescribed by negotiations with the U.S. Government; that is, to be more precise, the Prosecution made a request to the government that it be allowed to have Mr. Galbraith testify about certain topics and permission was granted for him to testify about those topics. So our direct examination is restricted to those topics and the cross-examination must also be restricted to those topics. The second condition that was ordered by the Court was that a representative of the United States government is present -- be present here in court, and she is present. I would like to introduce her, she's seated her between Mr. Black and Ms. Valabhji, her name is Heather Schildge, her last name is spelled S-c-h-i-l-d-g-e. She is a deputy legal [Realtime transcript read in error "league"] counsel at the United States' embassy and is here representing the United States' interest in this matter. She is seated here only because there no other seat in the courtroom, but of course she is not a part of the Prosecution team; she is here on behalf of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You did say that she's deputy lead counsel not lead counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I am speaking too quickly. She is deputy legal counsel. With those introductory remarks -- oh, one other matter just to raise. Because of the changing schedule, I just want to alert the Court that we have managed to secure two witnesses for this week to -- this witness and another witness. I don't anticipate that we will be able to fill the whole week. We will probably end early. But I think the Court will understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now the government -- not the government -- resorting back to my old job. The Prosecution would like to call Ambassador Peter Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could the declaration be taken by the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Ambassador. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Can you hear me clearly through those earphones.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I can. Probably without as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, it's as you prefer. I think you'll find it easier to use the earphones.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you state your name, please?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Peter Woodard Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before I go into your background, just a procedural matter. Of course, we speak the same language and there are -- my questions, your answers, are being interpreted. In order for the interpreters to keep up, what we have to do is number one, not speak too quickly, which we both will probably forget at times, but we have to try to remember. And secondly, and maybe even more importantly, we have to insert pauses. So when my question finishes, just count to two or so and -- before you answer, and I'll do the same after you finish your answer. Okay?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Just going to go through your background and quickly lead you through it. You were born on the 31st of December, 1950, you received your bachelor's degree from Harvard university in the United States, a masters degree from Oxford University, a law degree, JD, from Georgetown University, also in the United States. From 1979 until 1993 you were the senior advisor to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in the United States. From the 24th of June, 1993, until the 3rd of January, 1998, you were the United States' ambassador to Croatia, which is why you still retain the title Ambassador. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you now questions about your time as the United States Ambassador, and I'm going focus first on your meetings with various persons during that time. First of all, can you tell us where you were stationed as the United States Ambassador? Where was the embassy?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was in Zagreb, the capital, located on Andrije Hebranga street, in the downtown part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And during the time that you served as United States Ambassador, can you tell us approximately how frequently would you meet with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: In the first two years that I was ambassador, that is to say from 1993 -- well, through the end of 1995 I met with him very frequently, several times a week, sometimes several times a day. After the end of 1995 our relations became more strained and I saw him much less frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During that time period while you were United States Ambassador, how frequently did you meet with representatives of the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina, RSK?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Less frequently, but from the period from March of 1994 until August of 1995, I was a principal in the peace process that attempted to find a settlement between the RSK and Croatia. So I would meet with various figures from the RSK once a month, or once every other month. Then in September and October of 1995 I was involved in a shuttle diplomacy between Zagreb and the local authorities in Eastern Slavonia. At this point they were no longer calling themselves the RSK and I saw them very, very frequently in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us why, Ambassador, the RSK was generally referred to as the, "So-called RSK'?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Because it was the self-styled Republika Srpska Krajina, it was not recognised by anybody in the world, and every country accepted that -- recognised that this territory was part of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, Ambassador, when you first met Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: In April of 1994 I went down to Knin, and I met him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in what capacity -- what position did he hold at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: At that time he considered himself to be the president of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many times after that first time you met with Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Maybe five or six times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did those meetings occur?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: In Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How would you get to Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I would -- well, the first time I went down, I drove. Afterwards I would go typically by helicopter. That was a flight that UNPROFOR provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you first met with Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: On the 23rd of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was his position at that time, when you met with him?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He was the foreign minister of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions now about what you refer to as the peace process that you engaged in. Did that have another name?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was -- the name that was commonly associated with it was the Zagreb 4 process which was then shortened to the Z-4 process. It began as a -- perhaps I should explain. The Z-4 were the United States, the European Union, the Russian Federation, and the United Nations. And I was the American representative in that process. It began with cease-fire negotiations in the Russian embassy that were hosted the 19th of March 1994 by the Tali Vitaly Churkin, the Russian deputy foreign minister. Those negotiations concluded successfully on the 30th of March, 1994, and those of us who were sponsoring those negotiations, the same, the Z-4, felt that we needed to continue the momentum. So the first phase was the cease-fire; the second phase was in an effort to reach an agreement on economic and confidence-building measures between Zagreb and Knin; and then the final stage was intended to be a political plan, which would have provided for the peaceful reintegration of the Krajina and Slavonian regions into Croatia in circumstances that gave the Serb-majority areas very substantial autonomy. The Z-4 plan, as distinct from the Z-4 process, refers to the last phase, namely the effort to find a political solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. I want to ask you about the first phase, the cease-fire, which you said was concluded successfully on the 30th of March, 1994. Can you tell us what -- what was the positions of the various sides with respect to that cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: There was a broad agreement between the Croatian side and the Knin authorities that there should be a cease-fire. The issue related to the modalities of the cease-fire, what was the separation zone, where could police go, what kind of identification they would have to have, and then a political issue where the Croatians wanted a statement that basically recognised that this was part of Croatia in the chapeau to the agreement. But because both sides actually wanted a cease-fire, we were able to work those issues out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in your earlier answer, you said that the final stage was intended to be a political plan that was -- would have provided for substantial autonomy for the Serb-majority regions. What regions were -- did that include?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Basically it was the greater part of what was known as sectors north and south of the UN-protected areas. So Knin, Petrinja, these areas. It did not include -- it did not include western or Eastern Slavonia, which had not had a Serb majority as of the 1991 census. And we operated -- when we spoke of Serb majority areas, we operated off of the pre-war census, since obviously these areas were almost purely Serb thanks to the ethnic cleansing that had taken place in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the cease-fire was achieved on the 30th of March, 1994. And you told us what was contemplated to occur after that, the second phase and the third phase. Can you tell us what, in fact, happened, if anything, after the cease-fire was achieved on the 30th of March, 1994?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was a very difficult process that followed. The negotiations were meant to resume two weeks later, that is in the middle of April in 1994. And the Serbian side, the RSK authorities, began to play all sorts of games, reasons that they were not going to have substantive negotiations. Just to illustrate what happened with the first round, after the -- there were two rounds for the cease-fire. 19th of March 29t of March 1994 at the embassy. At the 19th of March round, the Serbian side asked if they could bring journalists to the next round. And the Croatian side agreed. They brought two journalists which is possibly as many journalists that they had. When it came time for the April round, which was going to be at Plitvice in the Serb-occupied territory, the Croatians wanted to bring five journalists, which actually represented a major effort on their part to bring the smallest possible number of journalists, but they wanted one print journalist, one radio, television man and so on. The Serbian side said -- refused, said we only had two - although the Croatians hadn't limited; simply the number they wanted to bring - you only get to bring two. And it was this kind of games that then led to the cancellation of the trip and, in fact, that is why I made my first trip down to Knin, which I think was April 11th, 1994, to try to persuade the Serbian side to go ahead with the meeting. Of course I was unsuccessful. This process dragged on, that is the economic and confidence-building measures from April of 1994 until December of 1994, when an agreement was eventually reached. But as it dragged on, the Croatian side was losing patience with the whole peace process.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you went down to -- to make that first trip to Knin, that was when you met Milan Martic for the first time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you tell us what was Milan Martic's attitude towards the Z-4 process at that time, specifically towards the economic and confidence-building measures?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He was, in my judgement, not supportive of that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know why he was not supportive?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He was opposed to -- he was opposed to any relationship between Knin and Croatia. He imagined that the RSK could be an independent state or perhaps become part of Greater Serbia. He -- but the truth is, he was also, in my judgement, completely over his head. He didn't really understand anything about politics, international relations, negotiations, and he reacted, as people often do in those circumstances, by refusing to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you tell him about the Z-4 process and about the position that he was taking with respect to the Z-4 process?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I warned him repeatedly that this would end up in a catastrophe for the Krajina Serbs, as indeed it did. There was an opportunity to negotiate a peace agreement with Croatia that would provide substantial political autonomy, would give -- in which Krajina would escape the sanctions which applied to it. That the international community would help in the reconstruction of the region. And that if he refused this, the -- it was almost certainly going end up in a war, and it was almost certain -- it was certain that his side, which, after all, had about 180.000 impoverished people, was going to lose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you address his belief that the RSK could become an independent state or perhaps become part of a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I told him that would never happen, that there wasn't a country in the world that would recognise the RSK as an independent state, that the territorial integrity of Croatia was supported by the European Union - they were part of the Z-4 process - by Russia, which many Serbs had thought was pro-Serbia; nonetheless, the Russians supported the territorial integrity of Croatia; the United States and, of course, the position -- this was the position of the United Nations itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You told us earlier that you didn't have your first meeting with Milan Babic until the 23rd of January 1995. Nonetheless, did you have occasion to learn, during 1994, what Milan Babic's position was with respect to the Z-4 process, and specifically the economic and confidence-building measures?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to see Milan Babic in 1994, but he wouldn't see me. He was opposed to the economic and confidence-building measures. I think his opposition was not intrinsic to the substance of those negotiations or the substance of the agreement that emerged, but he was a bitter political rival of Milan Martic. He felt, correctly, I think, that Martic had stolen the 1993, 1994 presidential election from him. And he was determined to use the negotiations as a club against -- a political club against Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to anticipate some future questions, did Milan Babic's position with regard to the Z-4 process ever change?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Very radically. Not on the necessarily on the economic and confidence-building measures, which was an agreement that was concluded on December 2nd, 1994, but in January of 1995, 23rd of January, I met him for the first time. I outlined to him the substance of the Z-4 political plan; that is, the plan that would have reintegrated Krajina into Croatia, giving very substantial autonomy to the Serb-majority areas, and he was very interested in that plan. Subsequently I saw him in March of 1995. He accepted the plan, physically took it. Not accepted the substance, but agreed to look at it, agreed to receive it. And then I saw him again on the 2nd of August, 1995, and he agreed to accept the plan in substance. That is, that he would accept the idea of reintegration into Croatia, although by the 2nd of August he clearly understand that it would be much less autonomy than had been suggested in the Z-4 plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On the 23rd of January, 1995, when you met with Milan Babic, did you actually give him a copy of the plan, or did you just outline it for him?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: No, I just discussed it in outline form. We were waiting until the 30th of January to make the formal presentation, both to the Croatian side and to the Serbian side. So this was a -- really an effort to prepare the ground for that formal presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did that meeting occur in Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you, after your meeting with Milan Babic, were you supposed to meet with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I was supposed to meet with Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He sent word that he was cancelling the meeting because I had violated protocol by meeting with the foreign minister before meeting with the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So did you meet with him that day?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did not meet with him that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened on the 30th of January?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: On the 30th of January, in the morning, the Z-4, so the Russian ambassador, myself, several European Union ambassadors, United Nations representative, we went to -- first up to see President Tudjman in the presidential palace in Zagreb. We made a presentation about the plan, we presented the plan to him, handed it over, and I can tell you that he did not like the plan. But he did what we asked. Namely, he agreed that he would negotiate on the basis of the plan. The plan was never a take it or leave it proposition, it was simply intended as a document to be the basis of negotiation. We then flew down to Knin where, in the late afternoon, early evening, we met with the leadership of the RSK in the castle in Knin. That was their headquarters. We made a presentation about the Z-4 plan. The Russian ambassador then attempted to hand it to Milan Martic, and he refused to receive it. He refused to touch the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us who else was present at that meeting from the RSK side?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. Milan Babic was there, as was the -- Prime Minister Nikolic, among others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Milan Martic explain why he was refusing to take the document?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. He said -- the Croatians had, at the beginning of January, announced that they would not extend the UNPROFOR mandate beyond its expiration date which I think was the end of March of 1995. And he said that he would not negotiate until -- unless the Croatians agreed to extend the UNPROFOR mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the UNPROFOR mandate was, in fact, extended?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: In March of 1995 this was a product of American diplomacy led by assistant second Richard Holbrook. We -- Holbrook had come to Zagreb and we had gotten the Croatians to agree in principle to -- to agree to an extended United Nations mandate. There were cosmetic changes. Among them the name was changed from the UN mission from UNPROFOR to UNCRO which -- well, it was meant to convey United Nations in Croatia, but it had some other -- the CRO had another word -- set of words that went with it, cooperation, reconstruction, I forget the details. But basically the mandate was continued until the 1st of December, 1995, and that deal was sealed in a meeting, the social summit in Copenhagen, where vice-president Gore met with President Tudjman. Holbrook, myself were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was in March of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After that occurred, did Milan Martic accept the Z-4 plan and agree to engage in the Z-4 negotiation process?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Going back to the meeting of 30th of January, 1995, when Milan Martic refused to accept the document, how did you react?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: We spent two hours trying to persuade the Serbian side to reconsider. We explained that they were not committed -- by accepting the document, by agreeing to negotiate on it, they were not committed to any of the terms of the document. We tried to explain that if they refused to engage in the peace process that -- that they would increase greatly the chance of a renewed conflict. We tried to explain that the -- I explained that the international community had limited patience. That, after all, they had here the most powerful countries in the world, and certainly the most powerful ones operating in the Balkans, that this was an opportunity and that the opportunity would not always be there. And I made these arguments, the Russian ambassador made these arguments, the European Union representatives made these arguments, and it had no effect whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the meeting ended?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: At the end of the meeting the Prime Minister Nikolic, who was sitting next to Martic, looked at us and he said, "You think that you are professional diplomats, but you have made a huge mistake."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you say, if anything?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I looked at him and I looked at Martic and I said, "A huge mistake has been made, but we will see who has made it."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Milan Babic say anything at the end of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: As we were leaving, shaking hands, he came up to me and he said, in English, "I'm sorry."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I understood it to mean that he recognised that this was a huge mistake on the part of the leadership of the RSK, and that an opportunity was being lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you try to present the plan to Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That -- the idea was that we would present the plan to Tudjman, to the RSK leadership, and to Milosevic. Milosevic said that he would not receive the plan, and he would not receive the Z-4 delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know why Slobodan Milosevic opposed the plan, or the process?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Milosevic supported part of the process, namely the cease-fire arrangements, agreement, and the economic and confidence-building measure. I can give you my informed opinion as to why he refused the Z-4 plan, which is that he was very much afraid that the level of autonomy that was being promised to the Serbs in Krajina under the plan would set a precedent for Kosovo, and he did not want to see that take place. I also believe that by January of 1995, or even 1994, he had already decided that he would give up the Krajina, and that he -- that he wanted to trade, if you will, the Krajina for other territory, possibly Eastern Slavonia and territory in Bosnia. And therefore, he was not particularly interested in seeing a peace agreement between Zagreb and the Serbs in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when you say that he had already decided that he would give up the Krajina by that time, by January of 1995, or even 1994, did that represent, to your knowledge, a change in his position?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. I think when the wars of the former Yugoslavia began in 1991, that his dream of a Greater Serbia included Eastern Slavonia, it included the Krajina, and included Dubrovnik and the region around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know why his position would have changed between that time, 1991 wars, and what you described earlier -- what you described in your previous answer, January 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I can again only offer an informed opinion, but what happened in between was that there was international recognition of Croatia and of Bosnia, and international sanctions on Serbia of increasing effectiveness. And it became clear to Milosevic that there was no possibility that the world was going to accept changes in these borders. So therefore, the dream of a Greater Serbia was -- was disappearing, and that the most that he might hope for were smaller territorial changes by agreement with the Croatians. And I think he had the thought that he might be able to get Eastern Slavonia and, frankly, I think David Owen, the -- one of the international mediators encouraged him in the belief that he might be able to get a border change that would give him some Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to just look at the Z-4 plan itself that you -- that you presented to the parties on the 30th of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter Exhibit 351 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see that in front of you, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you tell us what that is, if we could scroll down on the page there.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is a code cable from Thorvald Stoltenberg, who was the UN representative in this process, and he is attaching to it a copy of the Z-4 plan with some of the final modifications that were made following a meeting in my residence in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is this the plan that was presented to the parties on the 30th of January, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: If it is -- it is the plan or it is extremely close to the plan. There might have been some minor changes even after this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just want to look at a few provisions of the plan. And as we're doing that, if you -- if you think of any of the changes that might have occurred, let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But if we could look at page 9 first. And if we could just scroll down to Article I.3, "Flags and emblems."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The plan, the proposal would have allowed the Krajina to adopt its own emblem and flag?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct. This was a very important issue for the Serbs, who wanted to have their own symbols so they could have the Serbian flag, and that was permitted under the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at the next page, please? At the top, Article I.4, "Language," the use of the Serbian language and Cyrillic script was also provided for?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look at the next page, please. At the bottom of point 2 there, it's a list of competencies that would fall under the government of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And education, culture, housing, public services, and if we could now go to the next page, because that list continues. And there -- I won't go through all of them, business, charitable activities, energy and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could go to page 14, please. There on the -- scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Article III.1 provides for a legislature in the Krajina government?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, please. There, Article III.2 provides for a president and various provisions for the president of the Krajina. That was also provided for?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could that be admitted into evidence and given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. Could a number be assigned be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 381, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, you have touched on this indirectly in some of your answers, but I want to ask you more directly now about Slobodan Milosevic's relationship with the leaders of the -- of the so-called RSK you referred earlier about the presidential elections that were held in the RSK in the 1993 and the beginning of 1994. Did you -- first of all, if you could tell us what happened to your knowledge in these elections and, secondly, of what Milosevic's role, if any, was in those elections?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: The elections were a two-stage process. The first round in December of 1993, and a run-off in January, if I have that -- those dates correctly. In the December round Babic got I think around 49 per cent of the vote, Martic in the mid-20s. In the second round Martic had 53 per cent, and Babic had 47 per cent. Now, in the history of democratic elections I don't think you will find a case where a candidate who is that far behind has been able to overtake, in a second round, a candidate who almost had a majority. And, indeed, Babic's strength was confirmed by the fact that his party won the parliamentary elections for the RSK assembly. Based on the reporting that we had from a variety of sources, we believed that the election was rigged, and rigged with the active participation of the Serbian authorities, presumably acting under Milosevic's instructions. Milosevic did not like Babic. He -- his preferred candidate was Mikulic, but Mikulic had no basis of support in Croatia, so as an alternative to Babic, he supported Martic. When I saw Babic on the 23rd of January, 1995, he also told me that Milosevic had been responsible for rigging the election against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, do you know during the time that you were U.S. Ambassador to Croatia and the so-called RSK existed, do you know if the RSK received any financial assistance from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It received major financial assistance from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Of what kind? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: The Serbian government paid the -- paid for the army, that -- the salaries of the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina. I suspect they also paid for the salaries of the police. They provided fuel, and other essential commodities. The Krajina was an extremely poor area, with no -- very few indigenous resources, and so it was almost entirely dependent on a life-line that came through Bosnia from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in your dealings with the various RSK leaders that you've talked about, were you able to tell if they consulted with Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It certainly was my belief that they didn't do anything significant without consulting with Milosevic. Babic told me as much, and this, I think, became particularly clear to me when I was negotiating the Eastern Slavonia agreement, what became the Erdut agreement. This was the process that began in September of 1995, and ended successfully on the 12th of November, 1995, in which the Serbian negotiator, Milan Milanovic went to Belgrade to get his instructions after -- before every negotiating session and told me as much. And, in fact, we met in a room where there was a large picture of Milosevic on the wall, even though ostensibly this was a different country.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the shelling of Zagreb on May 2nd and May 3rd of 1995, was there a change in the army of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. The army commander was replaced, and I think because -- on Milosevic's instructions, because Milosevic was -- did not want to have another incident in which there was a shelling of Zagreb. And, indeed, during Operation Storm in August of 1995, there was no shelling of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who -- which commander was taken away, and which commander came in?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, Selekovic [phoen] was removed and Mrksic was installed in his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to go now to October of 1994 and specifically I believe it's the 24th of October, 1994, did you have a meeting with Milan Martic on that day?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did. I went down to Knin, and I meant with him in the castle in Knin and that was followed by a dinner in a restaurant on the grounds, the castle grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the meeting, what was discussed at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: The military situation was getting worse. There was, at that time, an offensive by the Bosnian Serbs supported by the Croatian Serbs into Bihac, rather similar to what happened in July of 1995. There was a danger that the Bosnian government forces in Bihac might collapse, that there might be Croatian intervention. There was growing Croatian impatience with the games that were being played with regard to the economic and confidence-building measure negotiations. And so I went down to try to get Martic to stop his activities in Bihac, and to engage seriously in peace negotiations because time was running out. And my message to him was that time was running out, and if they did not engage seriously in the peace process, it would end with war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did Milan Martic respond?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He -- he said that the RSK had the means to defend itself, and that it had the capability of damaging or destroying Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you think he was referring to when he said that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I knew what he was referring to, which was that they had rockets that were capable of hitting Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have further conversation about that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: At the dinner, which was a very friendly dinner, we were talking, and he said to me, said, "You are a young man, I am a young man, I like you, I don't want anything to happen to you, we can do business, I can't deal with Tudjman. So if things get tense, you should be in touch with me so that -- and I'll let you know when you should leave Zagreb".

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, do you know if -- do you know if he knew where the embassy was located in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He asked about where the embassy was located in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I told him that it was where it was, in Zrinjevac, and that it was in the downtown part of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When he said, "I'll let you know when you should leave Zagreb," how did you respond?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I told him that I could not abandon the embassy, I certainly couldn't leave Zagreb, and I told him that a rocket attack on Zagreb would be a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why did you tell him that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Because he clearly was threatening to strike Zagreb with rockets if the situation deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you said that, that when you told him that a rocket attack on Zagreb would be a crime, could you tell if he heard you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I'm sure he heard me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he respond?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He did not respond, that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's move ahead in time to May 2nd of 1995. Can you tell us where you were on that day?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I was in my office, and looking through documents and actually looking at some pictures I'd been sent at -- I think around 10.00 -- well, a little after 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did something happen?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: There were some explosions, and since this was the -- just after Croatian operation blitz, and I had firmly in my mind Martic's threat from the previous October, I concluded immediately that those explosions were rocket attacks on Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you referred to Croatian operation blitz, was that an operation that was also sometimes referred to as Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you heard the explosions, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I ordered the staff, the alarm in the embassy to be sounded and the staff to go to our shelter, which was in the basement of the embassy building, and that is where we all went.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall how long you stayed in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: A couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you do after you left the shelter?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: In the late afternoon I went out and looked at the sites that had been -- some of the strikes -- sites that had been struck by the rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall some of the sites?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you describe them for us, please?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, on Vlaska street, which is right by the main square, the Trg Jelacic, there was a car parked on the side of the road. There was a hole in the windshield of the car, and there was a note that had been left in the windshield that said, "I'll be back in 20 minutes". But the man had, in fact, been killed in his car by the rocket so of course he never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So what else did you see that day?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I went over to the school, a school that had been hit, in fact a school where the foreign minister Granic's children attended. And the playground and the side of the school building was sprayed with the pockmarks from the rockets. And the school authorities told me that the attack had occurred about five minutes after the morning recess had ended. I think there were a couple of kids that were injured at the school. But had the attack occurred five minutes earlier, there would have been -- it would have been a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a school for what age children, if you know? Approximately. Are we talking younger children, older children?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: As I recall, I think it was served -- middle -- middle school age, but I actually at this stage don't fully remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were you able to --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I also went and saw the -- the site of the -- I think of the explosions that had first caught my attention, which were just across Zrinjevac park about 100 metres from my office, where the rockets had landed on some cars and caused a fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you able to ascertain, and maybe you weren't, but were you able to ascertain what the reaction of the people in the street was, to this attack?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I think people were shocked and frightened, terrorised. I mean it was a beautiful May day, and nobody expected to have death raining down from the sky on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That leads to my next question. I think you have already answered this, but had there been any warning that there was going to be such an attack?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from the warning that -- the vague warning that you received?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: There was no warning that there was going to be an attack. This was totally unexpected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did something happen on the following day, May 3rd, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: There were another set of rocket attacks on Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where were you when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I was in my office again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you, on that day, observe any of the results of the attacks?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: We went again to the shelter, but then foreign minister Granic called me up and asked if I would go with him to the children's hospital, which was struck by a rocket. Over the objections of my security, I agreed to go and I travelled in Granic's car to the hospital. And we went into the hospital, we saw where the rockets had landed, it was, as I said a children's hospital. And even worse for me than seeing the physical damage caused by the rockets was the -- seeing all the children who had been evacuated to the basement, some of them with -- with critical needs, cancer patients, and that sort of thing. And of course these children were terrified.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there an official response from the United States to these attacks?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. On instructions I sent a brief memo to Martic, Mikulic, and Babic. It observed that these attacks had taken place in close proximity to the American embassy, and it observed that historically American presidents have considered attacks on American citizens to be attacks on the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when that memo or letter was sent?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I sent it May 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there any military justification for the attacks, for these attacks that you've described?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: These were terror attacks. There was no military justification for them whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to show you a map of downtown Zagreb, and it's -- it's ERN number 0469-9051.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it possible to -- is it possible to turn that so it's not side ways? There. And if we could move -- slide it over to -- so the right side is more visible. Now -- there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, and if the usher could assist the witness, we're going to try marking this electronically.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you will be given a special pen. And it's hard to see, so I think you have to do it -- you're going to have to mark on the screen to your left, I believe. I'm wrong about that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I can -- I think I can -- this strains the limit of my eyesight, but I think I can find the locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I apologise. So if you can mark where the U.S. Embassy was located on this map, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That's the -- it should be right here. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And could you put a number 1 next to that so we'll know that that is the location of the U.S. Embassy?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yeah. [Marks] It's sort of a 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, and there is no doubt about that, it's -- it is just below the D on Donji Grad on the map?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, the Chamber is not able to have the benefit of knowing where the witness is indicating.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Should it not happen that we also are able to see where his pointer is going?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely right, Your Honour. I have it on my screen, perhaps the usher could assist in terms of putting it on the right screen. I have it on English -- the map on the courtroom monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, I can see it now. We are most grateful. I don't know if the interpreters though would like to have further benefit, are they okay? They have indicated that everything is in order. Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ambassador, I don't know if you will be able to do this, are you able to mark any of the other locations that you've made reference to? And if you can't, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I can. If I make a 2 here, that's roughly where the rocket landed that was across the park from the embassy. And right here, 3, that's Vlaska -- on the south side of the street is where the car was with the man who had left the note, "I'll be back in 20 minutes," who was killed. I don't think I can find the school. I didn't refer to it, but here is the Croatian National Theatre which was another site that was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you've put a 4 there?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The children's hospital is -- the -- the school is, I think, to the east, and the children's hospital to the west?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To the east and west of what?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Of the embassy and indeed of the places I've already marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be marked as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It is admitted as an exhibit. Could a number be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 382, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that map now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would like to show you now a clip from -- from a video which is -- it's 65 ter Exhibit 1816. It's ERN number is V 0000449. We don't, however, need to have it brought up on the e-court because we're going to show -- we've put the clip into Sanction so that the transcript -- actually there is no transcript on this. But in any event we've put it into Sanction because we have just one little clip to show from it. Ambassador, I'm going to ask you to watch this clip and see -- I think the usher can be relieved of his immediate duty. So if we could switch over to Sanction, and Ambassador, if you could tell us if you recognise anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have we -- I think we need the assistance of the AV booth to switch over to Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could we ask the AV booth to switch over to Sanction?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's try it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't know if anybody is seeing this. No, nobody is seeing it. Your Honour, I think it actually -- this falls conveniently because we're right about the break. Perhaps we could take the break and we will address this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It might be a convenient time now to take the break to give you the opportunity to do that which is necessary. Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: We are now going to take the break until quarter to 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please do proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think we have sorted the technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So Ambassador, I'm going to show you this clip and see if you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it should be the computer evidence screens, which on our buttons is the top right button. If we could play that now There should be an image -- there it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, I believe there is some success now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, just for the record, the clip that we just saw shows some burning cars and some fire trucks pulling up to the scene. Are you able to recognise that location?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is where the rocket landed across the Zrinjevac park from the embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And approximately how far away is that from the embassy?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It's very close, around 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this video be admitted into evidence, please, and given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. Please assign an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 383, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before you proceed, this clip relates -- sorry, does it relate to the 2nd or the 3rd, for completeness, of May, that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ambassador, which day did that relate to?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is the 2nd of May, possibly the -- the first explosion that I heard when I was in my office, which seemed quite close.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Was it heard --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Honourable Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry. How long after you heard the explosion? Or was it simultaneous? Please tell the Chamber. Explain a bit more for me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You said that it was the 2nd of May, possibly the first explosion that I heard when I was in my office, which seemed quite close. So you are referring to the clip, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So what I am asking then is was this happening shortly after, and how long after, or was it simultaneous or please explain to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was -- there was an explosion that I heard in my office followed by some other explosions. We moved immediately, or quickly to the basement of the embassy. And I went and visited that site later in the afternoon, so actually after the fire was extinguished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: About how long after? You said you were actually in the basement a couple of hours, so please give an indication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I visited the site around 4.00 p.m.. The first missile struck at either 10.23 or 10.27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So just to be clear in that clip you recognise the location, but you did not actually see the fire burning?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did not see the fire, it had been put out by the time I got to the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to show some -- you some photographs and ask you if you recognise them. And if we could first bring up 65 ter Exhibit 1652. And I think we have to switch off of the Sanction. Now, I'm just going to go through some of these pages. This is the first page of this exhibit. And are you able -- are you able to recognise what this is? And if could you scroll down, please. And then actually, I'll go through the pages, if we could go through the next page. Next page, please. And the next page, please. Okay. Now, could we scroll down, because I just want to get the ERN number of this particular page. For the record it's 0031-2230. Ambassador, are you able to recognise that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I am. It was the school that was hit on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what do you see there on the wall, on the lower picture on this page?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: These are marks that are made by the force of -- of the rocket, projectiles that were in the rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is this the yard of the school?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is the playground of the school or the yard of the school, and you can only imagine what would have happened had it been full of children when the rocket hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we scroll up to the upper picture? There, that's -- there the yard is visible. Could we go to the next page, please? And this is ERN number 2231. Do you recognise these pictures?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it's the yard of the school, playground. And again you can see on the ground the marks that are made by the projectiles coming from the rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And for the record, the ground is depicted in the picture on the lower part of that page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Before you proceed, is it possible in some way for an indication to be given of the marks that are made by the projectile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: For the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try to circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]. There were quite possibly more. It's hard to tell from this picture what is a -- where the asphalt is gouged by the projectile and what is debris from the -- from where it's been gouged out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I was going to admit the whole thing into evidence, but I think we need to admit this now separately before we move on to another page, otherwise we'll lose the markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 384, Your Honours, for the photograph marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So Exhibit 384 for the photograph as marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And could we go to the next page of this document, please? This is -- if we could just scroll down to the lower picture, please. And this is page 0031-2233.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise that, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Assuming that it's in the same place it is, looks like one of the marks that's at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recall seeing those sorts of marks in the -- in the yard?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And then finally, if we could go to the next page, which is 2234. No, I'm sorry, I didn't actually want to see that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we admit this collection of photographs into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The collection of photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The ones that we have just been observing, unmarked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Could the photographs as a collection be admitted into evidence, and an exhibit number now assigned to them, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 385, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we now get 65 ter Exhibit 1644, please? And could we go to page 30? And if we could go scroll down to the bottom so I can just read out the ERN number of this particular page. This is 0031-2336. And could we then look at page -- at the next page, please? Which is 2337.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ambassador, do you recognise anything from these photographs on these pages?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the car on Vlaska street where the rocket projectile went through the wind screen and where the man was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, to be clear, when you saw this, was -- in the pictures we see there is a body next to the car. Was the body there when you saw this?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: No, there was no body. That had been removed sometime before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Could an exhibit number please be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 386, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we have now 65 ter Exhibit Number 1655? And if we could scroll down. And the ERN number of this first page is 0031-2466. And I'm going to ask that we look at the photographs on the first eight pages, this being the first page, and go now to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ambassador, do you recognise this location?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I do. It is the children's hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this is a hospital that you visited on the 3rd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: With Foreign Minister Granic, and in the hospital was deputy Prime Minister Kostovic [phoen] whose daughter had been -- was one of the victims of the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at the third page of these photographs. Scroll down, please. Could we look at the next page, please? This is the fourth page, and just for the record it's 0031-2469. Did you see this kind of debris in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at the next page, please? And go down to the bottom, please. Did you see this?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please? This is 0031-2471. Could we go to the next page, please? And finally to the last page, 2473. Did you see what has been depicted in all these photographs that we've shown you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. Damage caused by the rocket attack on the hospital, and I -- if you are looking at the lower picture on 0031-2473, I specifically remember this corridor with the windows blown out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence, and could an exhibit number please be assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 387, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'm done with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ambassador, in the -- after the first day of shelling, did Milan Martic, to your knowledge, make any statements in the media concerning the shelling of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He did. He took credit for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a television broadcast. It's 65 ter Exhibit 2262, and its ERN number is V000-0448, but we will be playing it on the Sanction because we have the synchronised transcript. So, Ambassador, I would like you to watch the broadcast and see if it looks familiar to you. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I wish to address you with a few words and tell you about the situation that has befallen us and what we plan to do to get out of all this. "First of all, I wish to tell you that I sincerely sympathise with all the suffering that you've endured. I have preferred the situation to be good and that I've come to attend a wedding in Western Slavonia instead of having to come here when you are in your darkest hour to explain how to get out of it and how to find a way out of all of this so that you don't wander around and so that we can keep our land. "We've had a meeting here with civilian authorities, the military leadership, and our archpriests. What Croatia has done to us is undoubtedly a crime which was supported by foreign powers, America, and Germany. This was not a matter of treason. It was only that our enemy had the upper hand at that moment and managed to take control of the motorway and of this part as you know. "But I'm telling you one battle does not mean that the war is. As a countermeasure to what Tudjman did to you here, we have shelled all their cities. Sisak several times, Karlovac, Zagreb, yesterday and today. This was done for you. But let me tell you that the attack by Tudjman's forces did not focus only on Western Slavonia. He also attacked Lika and Dalmatia. Lika managed to defend itself and in Dalmatia their forces were removed from Mount Inera [phoen]. "Today an ultimatum followed. If they continued to attack our besieged forces, we would continue to pound Zagreb and destroy their cities. Then they begged us to stop shelling Zagreb and said that they'd let our people out of the encirclement, which is what interests you the most."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ambassador, is this broadcast that you've just been shown consistent with the media reporting that you were aware of at that time on the 2nd of May, 3rd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is completely consistent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this video and the accompanying transcript be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The video and transcript are admitted into evidence. Please assign an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 388, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to now play a radio transmission, and here we'll just hear the voice and see the exhibit it is 65 ter Exhibit 1473 the transmission is T000-0250. Again we'll play it on the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ambassador, if he could just follow along and see if this is also consistent with the reporting that you heard at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Croatia halted its aggression. It was halted for one simple reason. After our ultimatum that we would continue shelling Zagreb. I don't have anything to hide. I personally gave you the order to counter Franjo Tudjman and his leadership for his order to carry out the aggression on Western Slavonia and commit a crime against the civilian population in Western Slavonia. My order to shell Zagreb ensued and I would say that was what influenced them most to hold the aggression. At the moment the aggression has been halted and we are now negotiating with the UNPROFOR. As you know, an agreement was signed so that our civilians and soldiers with their arms, they can pull out of the encirclement and cross into Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ambassador, was that radio transmission consistent with the media reporting that you were hearing at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was consistent with the reporting we had from the media and from other sources that Martic was taking credit for ordering the rocket attacks on Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this transmission and the accompanying transcript be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Transmission and transcript are admitted into evidence. Please assign an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 389, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we now have 65 ter Exhibit 1822, which is an article from the Herald Tribune. And that I need from the e-court, please. I don't have it on the screen, I don't know if anybody else does. I'm getting a shaking from the head. Do we need to switch from the AV booth, from Sanction over to -- back to the e-court? There it is. Could scroll down so the top is visible, please? The other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is an article from the Herald Tribune dated the 16th of May, 1995, so it's some two weeks later. Do you -- were you aware of this article in the Herald Tribune at the time.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Almost certainly I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to scroll down, please, and the article includes an interview with Milan Martic, and there on the right-hand column part way down it says -- if we could -- that's fine. It refers to the interview. In the interview Mr. Martic, and then it says -- he's quoted as saying, "I'm very sorry if civilian targets were hit because our aim was to hit military targets," he said. Now, do you recall him at this time, some two weeks later, making statements to that effect?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I -- I -- I'm quite sure that I read this article, either in the international Herald Tribune or in the Washington Post where it originally appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And with respect to that quotation that I just read to you from this article do you have any comment or reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Mr. Martic had long indicated that he considered an option to launch attacks on Zagreb aimed at damaging, or in his words, destroying the city. This is what he indicated to me on the 24th of October. He -- this was the same statements that he made in the radio and television clips that you previously showed. He had indicated to me in effect that -- that attacking civilian targets in Zagreb, attacking the city itself, was an option, a way in which the RSK could respond to an attack to Croatian pressure or to a Croatian attack on the RSK. Again that is confirmed in the clips from the television and radio broadcast, I think the television broadcast from the 3rd of May. Now, two weeks after the event, he's slightly changing his story that he's coming to the realisation that what I told him on the 24th was true, namely that this was a war crime and he could be held responsible. So he was attempting to find, after the fact, a military justification for the attack by suggesting that he was really after military targets in downtown Zagreb. There were not military targets in the area that he was hitting. It was an indiscriminate attack on the city. It hit a children's hospital, it hit the Croatian National Theatre, it hit a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could an exhibit number be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 390, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I am done with the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to move ahead in time, please, to July, August of 1995. Did there come a time when you learned that Croatia was planning military action against the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: On or about the 21st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know why -- did you learn why this military action was being contemplated?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. What had happened in the -- in July of 1995 was a series of developments that were --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you -- okay. Sorry. I'm sorry to interrupt. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I misheard you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Was a -- so let me just start. In July of 1995 the Bosnian Serb army had overrun Srebrenica, massacred [Realtime transcript read in error "had overrun"] some 7.000 men and boys, it had overrun another safe area, Zepa, and it, along with the forces of the RSK, was launching an attack on Bihac, that looked like it might prevail. This was intolerable for the Croatian government, as indeed was intolerable for the United States. The Croatians feared that if Bihac was overrun, that the -- there would be another massacre, that the survivors would end up in Croatia which already had been burdened by receiving some two million refugees passing through the country since 1991. That it would create a solid western Serb entity of the RSK, plus the Bosnian Serb territory, so it put Croatia at a strategic disadvantage and the Croatian government was not going to let that happen. They also saw that there was no prospect of a successful peace negotiation with the Krajina Serbs, given the attitude of the accused who refused to negotiate. And the -- so that basically what was going on in Bihac and what had taken place in Srebrenica and Zepa, provided them with an opportunity to launch a military action that would relieve the siege of Bihac and retake the Krajina, and therefore solve the problem of this break-away region of Croatia. And so they moved in late July to do just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us where Bihac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, before you appropriate, at page 42, approximately line 30, there is a sentence that says in July of 1995 the Bosnian Serb army had overrun Srebrenica, had overrun men and boys, and had overrun another safe area. Could I get a clarification there? That's a typo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
