utterances.text: That it's an error, what I said was the Bosnian Serb army had overrun Srebrenica, had massacred some 7.000 men and boys, and had overrun Zepa which is another UN-protected safe area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The Chamber is grateful, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us where Bihac is located?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Bihac is located in northwest Bosnia, it was a UN protected safe area. On the -- to the north and west of Bihac was the territory of the RSK, and therefore also of the Republic of Croatia. And to the south and east was Serb-held territory in Bosnia. It was -- it was, in short, completely surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said in your -- in an earlier answer that the -- that the attack on Bihac by Bosnian Serb forces and forces of the RSK was intolerable to Croatia and also to the United States. Why? Can you just explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, first, it was a -- well, let me -- for -- let me take those -- that question in separate parts. For the United States it was intolerable because this was a United Nations protected safe area, which was not being protected. And because we believed that if Ratko Mladic took over Bihac, he would likely do the same thing he had done in Srebrenica, which was massacre the men and boys, and that the population of Bihac being four or five times that of Srebrenica, we were talking about in the neighbourhood of 40.000 men and boys being -- in danger of being murdered. For the Croatians, it was intolerable because -- well, for some of those same reasons. But also because they did not want to have an influx of the survivors coming into Croatia, adding to the burden of refugees in the country already. And it also would have put Croatia at a strategic disadvantage. As long as Bihac was there, the Serbs -- that is, the Croatian Serbs, the RSK, and the Bosnian Serbs had internal lines that is they had to defend. So they had to have forces that were facing the Bosnian 5th Corps that was in Bihac. If that no longer existed, then those forces could be transferred to the border between the RSK and the government-held part of Croatia, and in addition, could be transferred to the fight against the federation, that is the Croat-Muslim federation in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the participation of the RSK forces in Bihac also, just to be clear, entail crossing or engaging an international border?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It did. They crossed the international border. From a legal point of view, Croatia was responsible for maintaining its international borders. What you had then was an attack emanating from Croatian territory on to the territory of another state for which the government of Croatia was legally responsible to prevent such an attack. The a attack that Martic ordered on Bihac helped provide a legal pretext for Croatia to take the actions that it did in launching Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What position, if any, did the United States take with respect to this anticipated military action by Croatia that you learned about on the 21st of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: We took no position on whether the action should take place or not. We -- I did -- I personally warned Tudjman, pursuant to instructions, that if there was military action he had an obligation to protect the lives and property of Serb civilians in the Krajina region, and also to protect the UN peacekeepers that were present in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, after you learned about this contemplated action on the 21st of July, 1995, did you have any meetings with any leaders from the RSK?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I met with Milan Babic in Belgrade on the 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us how that came about?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. It was clear that Croatia intended to take military action. The United States did -- did not feel that we could tell the Croatians not to do it because if -- because of the danger that the combined RSK and Bosnian Serb offencive would overrun Bihac with the consequences I have previously decided. So we basically took the decision that we were not going to provide not a green light, not a red light, but no light at all in terms of the Croatian military offensive. Nonetheless, it was the desire of the United States to find a peaceful settlement to the conflict in Croatia, if at all possible. So when I was in Brioni meeting with Tudjman on the 1st of August, I told him that I had been in touch with Babic, and that Babic had proposed that I meet him in Belgrade the next day. Incidentally, my original idea was to meet Babic in Knin, but Babic said no, you can't come here, Martic will not let you come. So we have to do it in Belgrade. So in the morning of the 2nd I flew on a UN plane from Zagreb to Belgrade. I met that evening at the American embassy with Babic and we had a -- a long discussion. I warned him that there was going -- that there was going to be a Croatian offensive, that the RSK had no support whatsoever, and that -- that he -- at this stage if they were to avoid a war, they had to accept Tudjman's terms for a peaceful reintegration of the Krajina into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recall generally what those terms were, and did you communicate them to Milan Babic in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did -- I do -- I -- I -- I do recall. I communicated five points to him. They were first in -- an immediate withdrawal of all RSK forces from Bihac and the stopping of offensive actions in Bihac. It was -- was the immediate reopening of the gas pipeline from -- that went through sector north, a commitment to open immediately the railroad that went from Zagreb through Knin to the coast, an agreement to start negotiation, I think within 48 hours, on opening the road through Knin, and an agreement for a political settlement based on the Krajina being reintegrated into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did Milan Babic respond?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He was very serious. He began by telling me that he fully understood why the -- Croatia was about to attack the Krajina and that he could not understand why his government was attacking Bihac. He --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he make any reference to the meeting that you had had with him and Milan Martic on the 30th of January, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He did. He said that he could not understand how it was that -- that they had behaved in the manner that they had, that Martic had behaved in the manner that he had, with regard to a peace plan being presented by the leading powers of the world. That was an -- and he -- he apologised for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he respond to the conditions and demands made by Tudjman that were communicated to you -- by you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He accepted the first four points. But with regard to the fifth, which related -- which was the peaceful reintegration of -- of the Krajina region into Croatia, he said that -- well, he asked about how this impacted on Eastern Slavonia, would that have autonomy. And I said no, under the Z-4 plan, Eastern Slavonia was -- would not -- had there been a transitional period of five years to full Croatian control, but it would not have autonomy because it was not a Serb-majority area under the 1991 census. That was a problem for him and -- but basically I said, look, let me propose this: Why don't you say that you accept the Z-4 plan as a basis of negotiation, but you have to understand one point. You will never get as much autonomy as was envisioned in the Z-4 plan. You might have had that chance in January of 1995, but that's lost now. And I need to tell Tudjman privately, from you, that you understand that the -- a final settlement is going to be -- resemble much more closely the autonomy that is envisioned in the Croatian constitutional law than ti will what is in the Z-4 plan. He said, "Yes, I understand that. I will say publicly that I accept the Z-4 plan, but privately you can convey that to Tudjman."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Milan Babic say anything about Milan Martic's position at the I am time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, I asked him. I said, "You've accepted this, but what about Martic, will he accept it?" And Babic said, "One sentence from Milosevic and he will accept it."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did Milan Babic say anything further about Milosevic and his position?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He said that he had been trying to see Milosevic and that Milosevic would not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I sent a report on it to the state department, I got instructions from the state department, I got instructions and Rudi Perina the charge d'affaires in Belgrade got instructions that we were to go and see -- I was to see Tudjman and Perina was to see Milosevic to ask for them to support the Galbraith-Babic deal. Babic was to make a press conference the next day, the 3rd of August, accept being the first four points, and accepting the Z-4 plan. I spoke to him that morning, and he confirmed that he would go ahead and do it. I flew back to Zagreb, I briefed the -- some of the key foreign ambassadors. I then went up and I saw Milosevic -- sorry, saw Tudjman at 5.45 p.m. I told him what had transpired in Belgrade, what Babic had said. And I urged him to delay military action for several days. I said -- he -- he expressed great scepticism about the sincerity, about Babic's sincerity, and also about whether he could get Martic and the other Krajina Serbs to go along. I said, well, I understand why you say that, given the experience that you've had in dealing with them, but why don't you just wait for a couple of days, and there are things that they have to do under this agreement immediately. If they do them, then you will see that they are sincere, if not, well then you still have the military option. But frankly, at that stage, it was too late. He didn't believe that -- that the Krajina Serbs and particularly Martic, would go along with this and the momentum toward war had gone too far. I met with him at 5.45. At 6.00 p.m. he convened his national Security Council and they took the final decision for war, and, well, the advance operations began later that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you -- did Milan Babic hold the press conference and make the public statement?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was it consistent with what he said he would do?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was consistent. I wish he had been a little stronger, but it was consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you said Rudi Perina the charge d'affair in Belgrade was tasked to go see Milosevic. First of all, why was the charge d'affair given that task?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: We did not have diplomatic relations with the federal Republic of Yugoslavia and so there was no ambassador. The charge d'affair was the senior American diplomat and he was the man who would normally deal with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you learn whether he was able to meet with Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He was not able to meet with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know why he was not able to?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: My understanding at the time was that Milosevic refused to see him because he did not wish to support this deal. Subsequently, in testimony in this Tribunal in the Milosevic case, I have learned that Milosevic says that he was on vacation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to look at 65 ter Exhibit 294, and ask you if you recognise it. If we could just blow it up so we can read it. Ambassador, do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What it is?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is a cable from the British ambassador to Zagreb, Gavin Hewitt, back to the foreign and commonwealth office to the briefing I gave him and the other ambassadors on the 3rd of August about my meeting in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review this cable?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is accurate. He was an extremely competent diplomat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to page 2, if we could go to page 2, point 8. If we could just scroll down, so we could see point 8, please. Here it says in point 8 about the middle of the paragraph it says, "Milosevic was being briefed by the American embassy in Belgrade." Could you just explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: At the time that I did -- did this briefing with the -- with the key ambassadors in Zagreb, I believed that Perina was going to be able to see Milosevic and therefore would be able to brief him on the deal that I had concluded with Babic, and hopefully get his support. I did not know at that time that Perina had been unable to see Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. Could a number please be assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 391, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally, Ambassador, you've been testifying today about your dealings with the -- with various officials of the RSK with respect to the Z-4 plan, with respect to events in Zagreb and the shelling of Zagreb, and now with respect to this meeting in July and -- or rather on August 2nd of 1995 with Milan Babic. And I just want to ask you if you could give us your assessment please from your experience and dealings you've described of some of the various leaders of the RSK and I would like to start with Milan Babic. Could you give us your assessment of him, please?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I think he was the only leader who had -- who had in his heart the interests of the people of the Krajina region. He -- at the end, when the -- when it was the -- a choice between making a deal and -- that might have enabled the people of Krajina to remain, and sticking with his hard-line position, he put the interests of the people first and he was prepared to make a deal. He was easily intimidated by Martic and Milosevic, he was -- I wished he had been braver, I wish he had been more courageous, but I at least think he had the interests of the people in his heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You -- you've described -- you made reference to his hard-line position. Would you describe him as a nationalist?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, could you give us now your assessment of Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I -- I thought he was a man of very limited abilities, limited intelligence, who was way over his depth as the leader of the Krajina Serbs. He -- I don't think he had the interests of the Krajina Serbs in his heart. He -- he pursued his own interests, his own position. Faced with what everybody in the entire world saw, everybody saw, as forces that were going to wipe out the Krajina Serbs, that they were going to be defeated, when everybody saw that Milosevic was not going to support him, when everybody saw that the Bosnian Serbs were not going to support him, he still refused to negotiate. He still refused a deal that not only would have enabled people to stay, but would have given them an enormous amount of self-government. They could have had their own flag, they could have had their own bank-notes. They didn't want to have the Croatian currency, the kuna, because they said that was the same currency that was used by fascist Croatia in the Second World War, but the Z-4 plan allowed them to have separate bank-notes, the way Scotland had their Scottish pounds. They could have run most of their own affairs. In fact, so much so that when I met with Babic he said, "This is too much autonomy. We don't want to have to pay our own pensions. Couldn't Zagreb do that for us?" He not only refused the plan, but refused to talk about it. In that sense Milan Martic was Franjo Tudjman's best friend and ally. He gave Franjo Tudjman the excuse that Tudjman wanted to take military action against the Krajina and an action that got the result that Tudjman wanted, namely that there would not be very many Serbs living in the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Galbraith, I am defence counsel for Mr. Martic. My name is Predrag Milovancevic. We will start now with what we call here cross-examination and we will touch upon some topics that might be important to the defence of the accused. I will kindly ask you to make a pause before you answer my questions to make the work of the interpreters easier. In the information you provided as your personal background, Mr. Ambassador, and in your response to the Prosecutor's questions, you said that you are -- have a degree in law. Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You've also explained that between 1993 and early 1998 you were the ambassador of the United States of America to Croatia with the seat in Zagreb. Is that correct, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that before you assumed the post of ambassador you were a person who dealt with diplomatic matters, were you familiar with the situation in the former Yugoslavia before your arrival there that includes of course the territory of Croatia and that of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time of your appointment as the U.S. Ambassador to the Republic of Croatia, was it the case that in a section of the Croatian territories there were United Nations troops deployed and were these areas called the United Nations protected areas?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I mistaken in saying that the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or perhaps I should say the so-called or the then Republic of Serbian Krajina, I'm referring to the political and geographical area there, am I mistaken therefore in saying that the Republic of Serbian Krajina practically embraced those areas that were under the then Serb plan and the resolution of the Security Council included in the United Nations peace plan for Yugoslavia and where the United Nations troops were deployed?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception that in sector west UNPA, UN-protected area, also included territory that was under the control of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. You stated that as soon as you assumed the post of ambassador you had frequent contacts with the president of the republic and the representatives of the state authorities there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You've also explained that in a period of time when a peace solution was being sought that was in 1993, and particularly in 1994 and 1995, you had weekly and even daily contacts with the Croatian president, Mr. Tudjman and, where necessary, even more frequently; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that to have been a normal practice for an ambassador of a country, to visit the president of the republic that often in view of the customary diplomatic practice worldwide?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I think it depends on what country you are the ambassador from and the circumstances in the place where you are serving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have explained that practically from September, October 1994 onwards a negotiation process or a peace-making initiative was launched in order to find a peaceful solution to the crisis existing at the time in Croatia and in the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I testified that there was a peace process that began on the 19th of March, 1993, and continued through -- sorry. That began on the 19th of March, 1994, and that continued through to the 3rd of August, 1995, to try to find a peaceful solution to the conflict in Croatia, between the Krajina region and Zagreb. The political component of that, the process that led to the so-called Z-4 plan, began in September, with meetings by the diplomats who were its sponsors, namely myself, the Russian ambassador, the EU representative Gert Arends [phoen] and Kai Eide, the United Nations representative and that continued until the presentation of the plan in January, and then of course there was the effort I described to try to revive it just before the war. There were, of course, separate diplomatic tracks that -- in which the United States was involved that were -- preceded this, that related to the conflict in Bosnia, both a diplomatic tract in which I was involved in the war between the Bosniaks and the Croats and a larger effort to try to find a peaceful settlement to the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you talked of the peace initiative which had to do with the Republic of Croatia where you were the U.S. Ambassador at the time, you mentioned three phases and for the first phase you said that it had to do with the cease-fire agreement which was the well-known Zagreb agreement, you said that it was dated 30th March of 1994, and I suppose we are referring to one and the same, the Zagreb cease-fire agreement that was reached in 1994?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is -- that is correct. The agreement is actually dated the 29th of March, 1994, but it was, in fact, concluded at about 3.00 in the morning on the 30th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification, Mr. Ambassador. This agreement that was reached in Zagreb between the 29th and the 30th of March, 1994, a cease-fire agreement, could it be said that this was an international agreement in view of the parties that had contributed to the reaching of the agreement, that had brokered the agreement, could it be put in those terms?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I would describe it as an agreement between two parties within Croatia that was brokered by international mediators. But the mediators were not parties to the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right, Mr. Ambassador, in saying that there were indeed two parties, one was that of the representatives of the Croatian authorities and the other of the representatives of the then Republic of Serbian Krajina, which two parties reached an agreement regulating the cease-fire with certain provisions as to how to separate the warring parties. Therefore, these were -- this was an agreement reached by the two sides that I've just mentioned, with the mediation of the international community?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is a correct characterisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This agreement was reached quite a long time ago. I am interested in hearing whether you recalled details of the agreement that the agreement provided for the following in view of the existing lines of separation, the warring parties had to be separated so that the pieces of weaponry had to be distant about one kilometre, one from each other, mortars at a -- had to be pushed back at a distance of 10 kilometres, whereas tanks and artillery had to be placed at a distance of 20 kilometres. Was this indeed the subject of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It's been a long time since I've looked at this agreement, so I couldn't say specifically a lot about the details. But I think what you have described sounds correct. Certainly I recall there was a one-kilometre zone in which all military forces were prohibited. I think one kilometre on each side of the line, actually, so it was a two-kilometre zone. And then there were other zones of categories of weapons, but the details I don't remember at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Basically you have answered my question. You do recall that the agreement dealt with the separation of the warring parties. My next question is the following: Do you know that for instance the Republic of Serbian Krajina had established commissions which had to deal with the separation lines, thee were commissions charged with discussing the -- these matters as to how to separate the warring parties with the other side that was signatory of the agreement. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't recall the details, but I believe there were joint commissions that were meant to work out some of these modalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Another brief question before we break. Mr. Ambassador, can it be said that this cease-fire agreement, complete with the modalities we've referred to, was in force from the period when it was signed, that's to say late March, 1994, up until May 1995, or the 1st of May, when Operation Flash was launched, that in this period there were no activities that constituted significant violations of the agreement? And I'm referring to both the Croatian and the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I do not recall there being significant violations of the agreement in the period that you describe. I do recall many complaints from both sides that the agreements were being violated, which -- part of which had to do with an ambiguity in the agreement about police in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this could be an appropriate moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: We will take the break now and come back at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, before the break we talked of the Zagreb agreement on the cease-fire from late March 1994. The next topic we will discuss now has to do with the agreement on the economic cooperation between the Republic Serbian Krajina, the then Republic Serbian Krajina and Croatia. You mentioned it as the second phase of the negotiations with a view to finding a peaceful settlement of the crisis. Do you recall what time of year it was -- rather it was in the second half of 1994, but do you recall which month it was when this agreement on the economic cooperation and trust-building between the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Croatia was reached?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was signed, as I recall, on the 2nd of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please take it just a little bit slower, having regard to the interpreter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The economic agreement was reached after the cease-fire agreement, therefore, and it envisaged measures for the establishment of economic ties which had to do with the oil pipeline and some other areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina held its meeting on the 30th of November 1994 adopted a package of -- of provisions, measures, concerning economic ties with Croatia, it was proposed by Mr. Mikulic, and do you recall the government of the RSK taking such a decision?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will put a further question to you in order to avoid misunderstandings in the transcript. In your response to the Prosecutor's question you mentioned in addition to Mr. Martic and Mr. Babic also Mr. Nikolic, but that should have been Mikulic, am I right, the then Prime Minister Mikulic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I'm sure that I said Mikulic and not Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the decision taken by the government, are you aware of the fact that the RSK assembly also adopted a text of the agreement on mutual economic cooperation and relations between the RSK and Croatia, this was in late 1994?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I -- I think that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony so far you explained that in January 1995 the so-called Z-4 plan was finalised. You explained that it stood for Zagreb 4 and you explained who the four parties were. This was a proposal for the peaceful solution of the crisis between the RSK and Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have also explained that you first offered the agreement to the RSK leadership in Knin, and that you turned to the president of the Republic of Croatia, Tudjman, later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. It was offered to -- it was proposed to the president -- to President Tudjman on the morning of the 30th of January, 1995, and then to the leadership of the so-called RSK on the evening of that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I must have misunderstood you. You offered the text of the agreement to both sides and you explained to us, is that correct, that this was not a take it or leave it offer, but an offer for political negotiations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct. The -- the proposal was meant to be the basis for negotiation. The idea was that the parties would look at the text, they would say the following points we can accept, we want changes in the following places. We would hear that from the Croatian side. We would then get the same reaction from the Serbian side. We would try to fashion a new text that accommodated as much of what each side wanted and continue that process until there was an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have explained that the RSK leadership did not want to receive the plan at all in January, 1995, that they had refused to physically accept it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I have an objection, and it's -- I would draw the Chamber's attention back to its order of the 13th of April. It says 2004, but I think it's supposed to say 2006. It's the Chamber's order that just came out with respect to conduct of the trial and specifically Annex A, point 3. The -- the order states that the parties are requested to avoid interpreting or paraphrasing what a witness has previously either testified or stated, and it goes on to give the reasons for that. I understand that sometimes it's necessary to quote back to -- in cross-examination to ask further questions; however, I would submit that every single question so far has been paraphrasing what the witness has said. And this last paraphrase -- sometimes accurately, sometimes inaccurately. The last paraphrase, I would submit, is inaccurate because the testimony is not that the RSK leadership did not want to receive the plan. As I recall the testimony it's that Milan Martic refused. So I would object on the grounds that the -- that Defence counsel is not adhering to what the Court ordered in its most recent order, and that this particular paraphrasing mischaracterises the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have anything to say that the objection that is raised by Mr. Whiting of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am aware of the order of the Honourable Chamber, and I've been trying, in dealing with a political topic about which the Ambassador is testifying, to get to the substance of the discussions that were held at the time, and I'm trying to put specific questions to the witness. Of course, if the Prosecutor objects to my questions, I can paraphrase them, I can -- rather, I can rephrase them, but it wasn't my intention to have the witness repeat what he already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It seems that there was a bona fide error in your referring to the RSK leadership instead of Mr. Milan Babic, which is accepted, but in future, please try not to paraphrase, to observe the terms of the order that was given. We realise that it's sometimes difficult, but try to contain yourself within the confines of the guidelines, if you will. Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I hate to be picky, but I think Your Honour may have misspoke when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, Martic and not Babic. I stand corrected. You are perfectly right, Mr. Whiting. Thank you. You've heard that, Mr. Milovancevic. It is, in fact, Mr. Martic. Please do continue. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, can you tell us whether the president of the Croatia, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, or the Croatian government, whether they ever accepted the plan, Z-4, that is?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: President Tudjman agreed to negotiate on the basis of the plan. He was not asked to accept the plan, and he would not have accepted the plan in the form that it was in. We knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you explained the reasons for which Mr. Milan Martic, as the president of the RSK, turned the plan down, you said more or less that he had pointed out to the problem of the extension of the UNPROFOR mandate in Croatia, and that issue was resolved only in March 1995; is that correct, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He -- he explained that the RSK leadership would not receive the Z-4 plan, would not physically receive the Z-4 plan or negotiate on it until Croatia agreed to extend the UNPROFOR mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After the UNPROFOR mandate was extended did you put forward the proposal to the leadership of RSK again?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Babic, and I gave him a copy of the plan in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you saw him and whether you gave him the complete plan or just a summarised version or a draft of it? Earlier on you've told us that only a draft proposal was presented to him.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: In March I gave him the complete plan. In -- when I saw him on January 23rd, 1995, I -- I -- I summarised the plan for him because the plan had not yet been formally presented, so we needed to follow certain procedures. And we were not going to give the plan officially to either party until we made the formal presentation first to the president of Croatia, since it was a plan that related to Croatia, and second to the leadership of the Krajina Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In March 1995 when you gave the plan to Mr. Babic, did you, either before that or immediately after that, present the same plan to Mr. Tudjman and what was his reaction, was it the same as it was in January?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: We had already presented the plan to President Tudjman on the 30th of January, so there was no need to present it to him again in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As regards Mr. Babic's reaction when you met him in Knin in January 1995, you also provided us with a detail he when Mr. Babic said that he was sorry as you were leaving, he said, "I'm sorry," that's quoting you quoting him. And in your testimony in the Milosevic case Mr. Tapuskovic as the amicus curiae confronted you with the European Community document dated January 31, 1995 in which it reads as follows: "Mr. Babic -- Babic's position was that the placing of Krajina under the sovereignty of Croatia would be something that would be decided by the population of Krajina." Are you ware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is possible that -- that Babic, in his public statements said something along those lines, but what I was testifying to was his reaction in a private meeting to a proposal that would have given the Krajina region of Croatia almost complete self-government, and he found that proposal to be a very interesting proposal, his attitude toward it was positive, because he believed it accomplished most of what the Krajina Serbs wanted -- what the Krajina Serbs needed, and at the same time avoided a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In response to my learned friend's questions about the contents of the Z-4 plan and the autonomy that was offered to the Serbs in Croatia, you explained that the area of the Eastern Slavonia and the Western Slavonia were not the areas that according to the Z-4 were areas that could have autonomy as a result of the 1991 census and the number of Serbs that lived in those two areas; is that correct, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Actually, there were different levels of autonomy. The Serb-majority areas in the Krajina, by which I am referring here to sectors north and south, they would have had a very, very high level of self-government. They also would have been areas, and this is very important, that would have been demilitarised; that is, the Croatian army would not have gone into those areas. It wouldn't have been the entire sectors north and south, because there were towns in there, like Slunj, which had a Croat majority and that -- at least the entire town of Slunj would not have been included. In regard to sector east, Eastern Slavonia, it would not have enjoyed that level of autonomy that the Krajina region would have had, but there were provisions for cultural autonomy and other rights for the Serbian community in that area. There was also a five-year transitional period to the restoration of a full Croatian sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you are talking about a significant autonomy that the Serbs would have been given, according to the plan, you have also told us that the -- that this did not apply to the entire area of the RSK but just some of the areas of sectors south and north. Can you be more specific and tell us what municipalities that referred to? What municipalities were to be given that kind of autonomy in the sectors south and north?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Most of the municipalities in sectors north and south would have had that autonomy. It would have been all the municipalities that had a Serb majority in the 1991 census. There was, in fact, a map that went along with the Z-4 plan, which we worked -- which we spent a lot of time working on. But we never presented that map, because we recognised it would cause a huge amount of controversy and we preferred the parties to think first about the levels of autonomy before we got to the specific areas that might be included. But the basic idea was the municipalities that had a Serb majority in 1991, according to the census, would be those that would be -- that would have the highest level of autonomy under the Z-4 plan, and if you provided me with a map that showed ethnicity in the 1991 census, I could list those municipalities for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We shall come back to the autonomy somewhat later, but now I would be interested in the following: You've told us what Martic's position was to the Z-4 plan, you've also told us how Babic behaved in January and how he behaved in March, 1995. And finally, you've also explained to the Chamber that on the 21st of July, 1995, or around that date, you arrived at a conclusion that Croatia was preparing a large-scale military operation. Is all this correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you are entering into the area of paraphrasing again and repeating what has been said by the witness previously without going on to another question. In essence, please try and serve the rules that have been laid down, will you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Once all this happened, when it comes to the attempt to present a plan, we arrive at the 1st of May, 1995. The Operation Flash and the 1st of May, 1995, do the two have anything to do with the Z-4 plan?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Not -- not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain your words, "Not directly," to avoid me drawing a conclusion from your answer, Mr. Galbraith. So can you explain your answer, "Not directly"?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: What happened was that the part of the economic and confidence-building measures agreement, that is the agreement of 2 December, 1994, opened the highway that went through sector west. There was a shooting incident at one of the rest areas, I think outside, just outside the sector west, and then in re -- I think a Serb was killed there. In retaliation Serbs, perhaps the local authorities, fired on motorists inside sector west. The Serbian authorities - Mr. Martic, actually - closed down the highway and the Croatians took advantage of his decision to close down the highway to launch a military action ostensibly aimed at opening the highway, but which was, in fact, intended to recapture all of sector west. Perhaps I need to continue to answer your question. None of that was directly related to the Z-4 political plan, but it represented a significant further escalation of -- of tensions that made it very difficult to resume a -- a political process. And furthermore, as you heard Mr. Martic explain in -- in one of the -- the television or radio address, no, sorry, in the interview he gave John Pomfritt of the Washington Post on the 16th of May, 1995, he considered Operation Flash to prove his point that there was no -- that it was futile to negotiate with the Croatians, that that was not something that should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the situation that you have just mentioned, and the events that happened on the highway, first the killing of the man, the retaliation, and then the highway being closed down, when did this happen, in what part of April, 1995? Do you remember that, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was at the very end of April, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact what explanation was given by the Serbian authorities or Mr. Martic as to why the highway had to be closed down on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I'm sure I was aware of it at the time, but I do not now recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the highway being open from Okucani through to Slavonia was the result of the economic agreement that -- dating 2nd December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can then one say that the Serbian side, the authorities of the RSK, honoured the agreement that the highway was indeed opened and that as a result of the incident that took place towards the end of April 1995, the highway had to be closed down as a result of that incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think I'm going to object to this question, Your Honour. I think the witness has answered that he -- I think he is addressed this to the extent that he can. He answered that he cannot recall at this time what Mr. Martic said as to why the highway had to be closed down on that occasion, so I think he has addressed -- I think it's been asked and answered, Your Honour. And also, while I'm on my feet, I think we're beginning to get very close to questions that are beyond the scope of the direct examination, which is a problem both in terms of the order of the Court of 13 April, 2006, ordering that questions stay within the scope of cross-examination, and also the specific order with respect to this witness, where it's even particularly important, because of the circumstances of this witness, that questions stay within the scope of cross-examination. I think we're very close to reaching that point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have anything to say in response to the objections taken by Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, given the first part of the objection, I will withdraw the question about the closing down of the highway. And as for the second part of the objection, that we are almost beyond the scope of the interrogation in chief, examination-in-chief, I would like to say that this incident led to the Operation Flash that was the subject of examination-in-chief. That's why I am putting all these questions, to lead me to Operation Flash and not to go beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting, the Chamber sees that you are on your feet. You did say "almost going beyond the scope".

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Of course there was a reference to Operation Flash because Operation Flash did immediately predate the shelling of Zagreb and was referred to as one of the reasons for the shelling of Zagreb. However, I don't think that that then opens the door for a full inquiry into all of the circumstances of Operation Flash, how it occurred, what occurred during Operation Flash, and so forth. The focus here is on the shelling of Zagreb. That was the focus of the testimony in direct. And while there is a reference to Operation Flash, and I can understand some questions, and I have not objected to some questions about Operation Flash, I will object quite strenuously to a full cross-examination and inquiry into all of the details of Operation Flash which I submit go well beyond the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Milovancevic accepts that. But, Mr. Milovancevic, what would be the purpose of your questions in relation to Operation Flash? Having regard to what Mr. Whiting has said concerning his manner of leading the evidence before the Court and its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Whiting put questions to Mr. Galbraith as to what he personally experienced during the shelling of Zagreb and he asked him whether the shelling was militarily justified and whether it represented an illegal act, an act that was permissible under the law. And by doing that, Mr. Whiting compels us to clarify the circumstances that led to that operation and why it was conducted in the way it was conducted. In other words, the Defence is adhering strictly to the subjects mentioned by Mr. Whiting. Mr. Whiting asked the witness to provide his opinion as to why the shelling was militarily justified and we have to clarify that. This is an -- a matter of essence for the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I -- I did not ask whether it represented an illegal act. I asked whether it was militarily justified. That's the first point. The second point is, I don't -- I don't understand how the questions into Operation Flash would address the issue of whether it was militarily justified because I can't imagine that Defence counsel would be taking the position that Operation Flash somehow provided a military justification for the shelling of Zagreb. So I don't -- so I don't see -- I don't see any connection at all between my questions and -- and substantial inquiry into what happened with Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Honourable Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I crave the indulgence of both yourself and Mr. Whiting for the Chamber to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. If the purpose of your questions is to respond to the issue of whether or not the attack on Zagreb was justified, then you may put the questions in relation to Operation Storm [sic] on the understanding that it's strictly limited to establishing that fact and that fact alone. So do not go beyond that and confine yourself and do not stray. That is the ruling of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, Operation Flash, not Operation Storm, I stand corrected. But you are to be confined in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, are you familiar with what happened at the meeting between the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, with the military leadership of Croatia on the 30th of April, 1995? At that meeting the decision was reached to conduct the Operation Flash on the 1st of May, and also upon the proposal of Mr. Tudjman a decision was taken to stage the highway incident in order to use that incident as a justification for the Operation Flash. Are you aware of that meeting and are you aware of the fact that those things were indeed what happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. It doesn't seem to me that this -- this is -- follows what the Court has ordered with respect to the scope. I don't see the -- I don't see it being with respect to the military justification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, what is the connection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the problem lies in the fact that Mr. Whiting claims that the Defence is trying to justify the shelling of Zagreb, which is absolutely incorrect, and it would make no legal sense, and in factual terms it would not be serious. We're talking about the reasons for the existence of a military act which can be either justified or not justified. I'm trying to establish whether Mr. Ambassador who was in Zagreb at the time when the Operation Flash started, whether he knows how this operation was planned and how it came about. In order for us to be able to understand Mr. Galbraith's answers we have to understand the behaviour of the side that conducted this operation, and I don't see it -- how it could be possible for the Defence to talk about the shelling of Zagreb if it didn't -- if it didn't point to the behaviour of the Croatian authorities at the time. We are only trying to reach an answer to the question whether there is a causal link between the two. We received an answer before from the witness that there is no military justification, and this is the part of the witness's testimony that we are compelled to clarify, to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You seem to be adopting a rather circuitous route that might not, frankly, be the right route. If you have a cause, you may put it to the witness, but you can't put it in a manner which offends the rules which have been laid down. So, at this stage, the Chamber's view would be that you should go no further here, unless you're going to be direct and put what you have as a cause to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will proceed with my cross-examination, respecting your instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, you've told us that on the 2nd of May you were in Zagreb in your office in the embassy, and that you heard an explosion. You've also told us that this repeated on the 3rd of May, 2005 [as interpreted]. Can you tell us at the time on the 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd, the 4th of May, you had information as to what was going on in Western Slavonia which was, at the time, a UN protected area.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, we had -- I had some information about what was going on in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what sort of information this was?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is just another way around the Court's order, Your Honour. And I would object. The issue is, what was the cause of the shelling of Zagreb, as the Defence counsel has put it, though the Defence counsel has also said that it's not -- he is not trying to justify the shelling of Zagreb, in which case I'm not sure what the relevance is -- becomes of the cause of the shelling. But the witness has already testified about this, has already said what -- and there is plenty of evidence what the cause was and that it was in reaction to Flash, so this is just further efforts to get into the subject of Flash and what happened in Operation Flash and so forth, which is beyond the scope of direct examination, it is also not relevant. It is not relevant to the issues of this trial, what happened in Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as a Defence counsel I find it difficult to put nonsensical questions. If that suited the Prosecutor, I would be able to do that. However, the witness stated that he was the American ambassador to Croatia on the 2nd and 3rd of May, and that the attack that took place on that date was not militarily justified. And every question I put to him, aimed at getting an answer to him as to what the basis was for his conclusion that the attack was not militarily justified. And if I'm not allowed to put such questions to the witness, then I'll simply have to desist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Are you saying that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Are you saying that the attack was militarily justified? Is that the Defence position? And are you further giving a reason for a military justification? Please answer me, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence is not yet at the stage when it can conduct examination-in-chief. It is merely cross-examining with a view to exploring a part of the testimony given by the witness to the Prosecution. The witness is not a military expert, but he was a very important person at that period in time in Croatia, and I believe that this sort of information that we can hear from the witness, whether there was military justification or not, could be of interest to both the Defence and Prosecution. We have already heard some Prosecution witnesses who had -- who talked about May 1995, there was Mr. Dzakula, there were others. I'm merely putting those questions that we deem relevant. We are trying to explore certain views expressed by the witness. There is nothing in what we are trying to do to point to what our submissions are, if any, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It has not to do with submissions, it has to do with your right to cross-examine in a particular way and on a particular area, an area that arose in the course of examination-in-chief, but in respect of which there are rules that say you have to be confined in a particular manner. If you are not going to be questioning to challenge the witness on the issue of whether or not there was military justification, and what that military justification was, then I do not think you can take it any further. You are entitled to put those questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, you were on the premises of the U.S. Embassy in Zagreb, it was in the course of the morning, on both the 2nd and the 3rd of May when the same situation occurred where you heard explosions. Can you tell us, what did you base your position on that the events involving explosions in Zagreb were not militarily justified? What was the basis for such a conclusion on your part?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: They were attacks on a -- a city, on civilian targets. There were no military targets in the vicinity, they were aimed or struck the national theatre, the children's hospital, a school, a main square, a street near the main square. I -- I thought -- I did not -- there was no military justification for striking civilian targets, even though there was armed conflict between the Croatian forces and the forces of the so-called RSK. And since, in my view, it was -- these attacks were not -- these attacks were intended to terrorise, and they did terrorise. Further, the accused had previously indicated to me that he would be launching attacks for the purpose of striking Zagreb, damaging Zagreb, destroying Zagreb, attacks that I understood, I believe he intended, were for purposes of terrorism rather than for any military reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you talked about the meeting with Mr. Martic at which he warned you that if the Croatian authorities led by Franjo Tudjman were to attack the RSK, actions were to follow against Croatian cities, did he tell you why he would fire upon the Croatian towns in that case, what would have been the purpose of such activities?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: The context of the discussion was that I had warned that the actions undertaken by the RSK, particularly with regard to Bihac, and the failure to negotiate were increasing greatly the likelihood of Croatian military action. I further warned that in my judgement the RSK cannot survive military action, a judgement that was completely vindicated by the events that took place in 1995. He was -- he responded to my assertions by saying that I was wrong, that the RSK did have the ability to defend itself, that it had an ability to attack Zagreb. So that really was the context of -- of his warning, and in essence he was saying we can deter a Croatian attack, or we can make it so painful that they -- because we can hit their cities and we can hit their capital, that they won't attack us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, since you are a fellow lawyer, have you heard of the term, "retaliation" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Reprisals, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: First, to be clear, while I have a law degree, I have never been a practicing lawyer. Second, I have heard the term "reprisals", but I do not believe it is legal or moral to have reprisals against civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So far we talked about the Zagreb cease-fire agreement dating from late March, 1994, we talked of the economic agreement, and you said that the territory of the RSK was, in fact, part of the UNPA zones. Was this particular agreement, the Zagreb agreement dating from late March, 1994, providing for a cease-fire, was it, in fact, in force in May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the area of Western Slavonia, which was the subject of Operation Storm, were there UN troops, UNPROFOR troops deployed there in late April and May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it's either a misinterpretation or counsel misspoke in the last question. There is a reference to Operation Storm. I think it's intended to be a reference to Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic, was it, in fact, a reference to Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I misspoke. I meant Operation Flash on the 1st of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many days Operation Flash lasted, and what happened to the Serb population in the area in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is -- this is beyond the scope of direct examination, and it's also not relevant. And for all the reasons that have been put forth before, and this goes beyond what the Court ordered, as I understood it, in terms of limiting the cross-examination to military justification. And here I don't see that in the -- in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My intention was to verify whether the witness, who was the U.S. Ambassador at the time, who was staying on the 2nd and 3rd of May on the premises of the embassy, which is outside of the area where the operation took place, whether he was able to assess the military justification of the event. My learned friend asked of the witness who held the position he held at the time, and was in the position that he was, to answer the question whether it was justified or not. My question was simply a follow-up on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Are you saying that Operation Flash constituted the substance for military justification? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please answer directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am trying to establish the causal link between the shelling of Zagreb and Operation Flash. I want to establish a direct causal link, and that's the basis of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: -- causal link, please tell the Chamber. I will see if I can help you. What is the direct causal link, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The direct causal link lies, Your Honour, in the fact that the first Prosecution witness examined in this case stated that the operation lasted on the 2nd and 3rd of May and beyond. And the second witness, who testified there, said that in the month of May, according to the official information, there were 180 victims in the area where the operation took place, and there were eight of them in Zagreb. And I was simply trying to establish whether the witness was able to conclude whether something was militarily justified or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Have any of those witnesses said that that fact therefore justified the military intervention, in the bombing of Zagreb, rather, and that it constituted justification for so doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not state that at any point of in time. It will be up to the Honourable Trial Chamber to decide that. The only matter I'm trying to assist the Trial Chamber in is to establish facts, those facts that this witness is able to testify about. This witness, in answering a question thus phrased by the Prosecutor, was not able to answer the question, because it went beyond the scope of his expertise, because he was unable to be that familiar with the situation on the ground, and I was merely trying to arrive at the basis upon which he deemed himself able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milovancevic, if, in fact, those witnesses did not draw the conclusion, I don't see how you can put it to the witness in that form. I repeat, and I think I have been very patient in the circumstances, the Chamber has been, if you have a cause, it can be put to the witness. You can confront the witness in this matter, in this manner. But I really do believe that it's time to move on, if you're not going to do it in the way that it has to be done. And I think the Chamber has to be firm now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, in answering my questions you stated that the Croatian authorities seized the opportunity they saw in the highway incident to capture Western Slavonia. Did they, in fact, succeed in capturing Western Slavonia through Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this capture of an UNPA zone was done in a forcible, military way?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object. This is -- the Defence counsel keeps coming back to the same question in one form or another, again and again. And I would submit at this point counsel is defying the order of the Court on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please abide by the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you were shown film where Mr. Martic speaks of the action when Zagreb was attacked on the 2nd and the 3rd of May. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In answering the Prosecutor's questions you explained that what Mr. Martic said was something you had otherwise heard and recognised as the reason, or rather as the way in which he is explaining the way things happened. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you confirmed that Mr. Martic had explained that the firing of the rockets upon Zagreb had prevented the further military operations and further suffering of the population?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: No. What I meant was that he -- he explained in the film clip that the bombing, the rocket attack on Zagreb was retaliation for the Croatian military action. That is what we understood from all of our sources to be his reason for doing it, and frankly, what I understood from my own conversation with him. That this was -- was an act of reprisal or of retaliation aimed at the City of Zagreb in response to the Croatian military action. And that is what he said in the film clip, and that is what I was confirming as my understanding -- as my understanding of his explanation. As to the consequences, I do not believe for a minute that the retaliation, that the retaliation, that the bombing of Zagreb, in any way was the reason why the Croatians stopped the military action, they stopped their military action because they had conquered all of Western Slavonia and there was no reason for them to continue further military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What you just stated is your understanding of what Martic had explained; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I understood Martic to say that he -- in that film clip, that he ordered rockets -- that he ordered rockets against Zagreb and that he did so in retaliation for the Croatian attack -- for the Croatian military action in Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question in relation to this situation. You said that Croatia stopped the operation because it had captured the entire zone. Do you know when it was that it did so?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It did so very quickly. The -- there may have been mopping-up actions that continued for some days after the initial military action, but within three or four days or a week it had full control over the zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What do you mean by, "mopping-up actions"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they moved militarily down the highway, took that, and then there were some Serbian forces that were north of the position that the Croatians had, and they captured them, maybe there were some additional skirmishes, but the operation was over very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Your view that there was no military justification for this operation, did you include in that position the report by the special UN rapporteur, Mr. Akashi as to what happened in the area at the time of Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object again, Your Honour. On the same grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that -- I think the witness has answered the question that -- with respect to Operation Flash, that it does not -- there is no military justification. And Defence counsel has refused repeatedly to answer the Court's question about whether it is taking the position that Operation Flash constituted a military justification for the shelling of Zagreb. And without answering that question, I don't think counsel should be permitted to continue asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as the objection concerning the question involving Mr. Akashi is concerned, I wanted to know weather the position put forth by the witness has his own position, the position of his government, or that of the United Nations. That was why I put the question to him. As for the latter part of the objection which has to do with the position of the Defence as to whether something is a justification or not, I am not claiming that Operation Storm [as interpreted] is a justification for Zagreb; rather, I am claiming that these are events which happened simultaneously and which definitely have a causal link between them. And now, as to which course the events, in fact, did take is something that we will learn from, among others, this witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Well, put it to him directly and get on with it and get over it, once and for all. What you have just told the Chamber, put that to the witness now, let us finish, and you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, in responding to the Prosecutor's question that there was no military justification, you put forth a position, a position that came from a former U.S. Ambassador to Croatia. Was this your private position, the position of your government, or the position you arrived at in consultation with UN representatives and other representatives of the international community?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was the position of the United States, that is of my government, that there was no military justification, no legal justification, in fact no justification whatsoever, for the shelling of Zagreb. That was also my personal position. I believe it is the position of the United Nations. And to answer your broader point, which I think I can do, it is my position and it was the position of my government that whatever human rights violations that were committed by the government of Croatia, and we were among the strongest critics of the government of Croatia over its human rights actions, and particularly its human rights policies with regard to the Krajina Serbs, that whatever their human rights violations were, and there were violations, that they in no sense, and in no way, provided a justification for the intentional killing of innocent civilians in a major Croatian city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And that would be directly related to Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That -- related to operation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What took place during the course of that conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whatever took place during the course of Operation Flash or in any other action, because this is also relevant to Operation Storm and other circumstances. In fact, there was also, Your Honour, a -- there were significant human rights violations against the local Serb population in Croatia, in the part of Croatia that was not included in the so-called RSK. All those things happened, we objected to them, but nonetheless, we did not in any way consider those to justify the ethnic cleansing or the rocket attack on Zagreb or any other of these actions that we considered to be crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that would answer your question, Mr. Milovancevic. And it is now time for us to take our adjournment, I believe. So I would hope that when we resume tomorrow you would be going on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence is finished with the topic today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And I think we can safely now take our adjournment and we will return tomorrow morning at 9.00.
